english: Over him crept feelings worthy of a leader who, with the snow now beginning to fall and mist closing over the mountaintop, knows he must lie down and die before morning. They faded the color of his eyes, and even in the two minutes it took him to walk the length of the terrace, they gave him the bleached look of shriveled old age. But he would not die lying down. He would find some crag of rock, and there, with his eyes on the storm, straining to the last to see through the darkness, he would die on his feet. R he would never reach.

De affarvede hans øjne, og selv i de to minutter, det tog ham at gå terrassens længde, gav de ham skrumpet alderdoms affarvede udseende. Men han ville ikke dø liggende. english: He stood stock-still by the urn, the geranium spilling over its rim. After all, he asked himself, out of a thousand million men, how many ever get to Z? Surely the leader of a forlorn hope, a doomed advance party, has the right to ask that, and to answer, without betraying the expedition following him, “One, perhaps.” One in a generation. Should he be blamed, then, for not being that one? so long as he has worked honestly, given everything in his power, until there is nothing left to give? And how long will his fame last? Even a dying hero may be forgiven for wondering, before he dies, how men will talk of him when he is gone. Perhaps his fame will last two thousand years. And what are two thousand years? (asked Mr. Ramsay ironically, staring at the hedge). What indeed, if you gaze down from a mountaintop across the long wastes of the ages? The very stone your boot kicks aside will outlast Shakespeare. His own small light would shine for a year or two, not very brightly, and would then be swallowed up in some larger light, and that in a larger one still. (He peered into the darkness, into the tangle of twigs.) So who could blame the leader of that forlorn party—which has, after all, climbed high enough to see the waste of the years and the stars perishing—if, before death stiffens his limbs so that he can no longer move, he lifts his numb fingers to his brow a little deliberately and squares his shoulders, so that the search party, when it comes, will find him dead at his post, a fine figure of a soldier? Mr. Ramsay squared his shoulders and stood very straight beside the urn.

Når alt kom til alt, spurgte han sig selv, af tusind millioner mennesker, hvor mange når da nogensinde til Z? Sikkert har lederen af et håbløs forpost, en dømt fortrop, ret til at spørge om det, og til at svare, uden at forråde ekspeditionen, der følger efter ham, »Én, måske.« Én i en generation. Skal han så dadles, fordi han ikke er den ene? når han bare har arbejdet ærligt, givet alt hvad han formåede, indtil der ikke er mere at give? Og hvor længe vil hans ry vare? Selv en døende helt kan tilgives for at undre sig, før han dør, over hvordan mennesker vil tale om ham, når han er borte. Måske vil hans ry vare to tusind år. Og hvad er to tusind år? (spurgte hr. Ramsay ironisk og stirrede på hækken). Hvad er de dog, hvis man ser ned fra en bjergtop over tidsaldrenes lange ødemarker? Selve stenen, som ens støvle sparker til side, vil overleve Shakespeare. Hans eget lille lys ville skinne et år eller to, ikke særlig kraftigt, og så blive opslugt af et større lys, og det af et endnu større. (Han stirrede ind i mørket, ind i det filtrede net af kviste.) Så hvem kunne bebrejde lederen af det håbløse forpost — som trods alt er klatret højt nok til at se årenes ødemark og stjernerne gå under — om han, før døden stivner hans lemmer, så han ikke længere kan røre sig, løfter sine følelsesløse fingre til panden en smule bevidst og retter skuldrene, så eftersøgningsholdet, når det kommer, vil finde ham død på sin post, en flot skikkelse af en soldat? Hr. Ramsay rettede skuldrene og stod ganske rank ved siden af urnen.

english: But his son hated him. James hated him for coming up to them, for stopping and looking down at them; for interrupting them; for the lofty exaltation of his gestures; for his magnificent head; for his demands and his egotism (for there he stood, insisting that they attend to him). Most of all, though, he hated the twang and twitter of his father’s emotion, which quivered all around them and upset the perfect simplicity and good sense of the way things were between him and his mother. He stared hard at the page, hoping that would make his father move on; he pointed his finger at a word, hoping to win back his mother’s attention, which, he knew with anger, wavered the moment his father stopped. But no. Nothing would make Mr. Ramsay move on. There he stood, demanding sympathy.

english: As he walked away, every beat of this pulse seemed to enclose her and her husband together, and to give each of them the comfort that two different notes, one high and one low, seem to give each other when they are struck at once and blend. But as the resonance faded, and she went back to the fairy tale, Mrs. Ramsay felt not just tired in body (she always felt this afterward, never at the time); her physical tiredness was also tinged with some faintly unpleasant feeling that had a different source. Not that she knew exactly what it came from as she read aloud the story of the Fisherman’s Wife. Nor would she let herself put her discontent into words when she saw—at the turn of the page, when she paused and heard, dully, ominously, a wave fall—what its source was. It was this. She disliked feeling, even for a second, that she was finer than her husband; and, beyond that, she could not stand being less than entirely sure, when she spoke to him, that what she said was true. The universities and the people who wanted him, the lectures and the books, and how supremely important they all were—none of that did she doubt for a moment. What unsettled her was the relationship between them, and the way he came to her like that, in the open, where anyone could see. Because then people said he depended on her, when they must surely know that he was by far the more important of the two, and that what she gave the world was nothing next to what he gave it. But then there was the other thing too: that she could not tell him the truth. She was afraid, say, about the greenhouse roof and how much it would cost to repair, fifty pounds perhaps; and about his books, afraid he might guess what she half suspected, that his latest book was not quite his best (she had picked that up from William Bankes); and then there were the small everyday things she hid, and the children noticing, and the weight it put on them. All this took away from the whole joy, the pure joy, of the two notes sounding together, and made the sound die in her ear now with a dreary flatness.
danish_before_fix: Mens han gik væk, syntes hvert slag af denne puls at omslutte hende og hendes mand sammen og give dem hver især den trøst, som to forskellige toner, en høj og en dyb, synes at give hinanden, når de slås an samtidig og smelter sammen. Men da klangen døde hen, og hun vendte tilbage til eventyret, følte fru Ramsay sig ikke bare træt i kroppen (det gjorde hun altid bagefter, aldrig i øjeblikket); hendes legemlige træthed var også tilsat en svagt ubehagelig følelse med en anden kilde. Ikke at hun præcis vidste, hvad den stammede fra, mens hun læste højt historien om Fiskerens Kone. Hun ville heller ikke lade sig selv sætte sin utilfredshed i ord, da hun så — ved sidevendingen, da hun holdt inde og hørte, dumpt, uhyggeligt, en bølge falde — hvad dens kilde var. Det var dette. Hun brød sig ikke om at føle, selv et sekund, at hun var finere end sin mand; og hinsides det kunne hun ikke udstå at være mindre end helt sikker, når hun talte til ham, på at det, hun sagde, var sandt. Universiteterne og de mennesker, der ville have ham, forelæsningerne og bøgerne, og hvor uendelig vigtige de alle var — intet af det tvivlede hun et øjeblik på. Det, der gjorde hende urolig, var forholdet mellem dem, og den måde han kom til hende på, sådan, åbent, hvor enhver kunne se det. For så sagde folk, at han var afhængig af hende, når de dog sikkert måtte vide, at han var langt den vigtigste af de to, og at det, hun gav verden, var intet ved siden af, hvad han gav den. Men så var der også det andet: at hun ikke kunne fortælle ham sandheden. Hun var bange, for eksempel, for drivhustaget og hvor meget det ville koste at reparere, halvtreds pund måske; og for hans bøger, bange for at han kunne gætte, hvad hun halvt anede, at hans seneste bog ikke helt var hans bedste (det havde hun fra William Bankes); og så de små hverdagsting, hun skjulte, og børnene, der lagde mærke til det, og den byrde det lagde på dem. Alt dette tog fra helheden, den rene glæde ved de to toner, der klang sammen, og fik lyden til at dø hen i hendes øre nu med en trist fladhed.

english: He made no answer. He took opium. According to the children, it had stained his beard yellow. Perhaps it had. What was plain to her was that the poor man was unhappy, and that he came to them every year to escape; and still, every year, she felt the same thing: he did not trust her. She would say, “I’m going into town. Can I get you stamps, paper, tobacco?” and feel him flinch. He did not trust her. His wife was to blame. She remembered the wicked way his wife had treated him, which had turned her, Mrs. Ramsay, to steel and adamant right there in that horrid little room in St. John’s Wood, when she had watched with her own eyes as that hateful woman turned him out of the house. He was untidy; he spilled things on his coat; he had all the tedious habits of an old man with nothing in the world to do; and his wife turned him out of the room. In her hateful way she said, “Now, Mrs. Ramsay and I want to have a little talk together,” and Mrs. Ramsay could see, as clearly as if they were before her eyes, the endless miseries of his life. Had he enough money for tobacco? Did he have to ask his wife for it? Half a crown? Eighteen pence? Oh, she could not bear to think of the small humiliations that woman put him through. And always now (she could not guess why, unless it came from that woman somehow) he shrank away from her. He never confided in her. Yet what more could she have done? A sunny room had been set aside for him. The children were kind to him. Not once had she shown any sign that he was unwelcome. In fact she went out of her way to be friendly. Do you want stamps, do you want tobacco? Here’s a book you might enjoy, and so on. And after all—after all (at this point, without being aware of it, she drew herself up, and the sense of her own beauty, so seldom present to her, came to her now)—after all, she did not usually find it hard to make people like her. There was George Manning, for example; Mr. Wallace; famous men though they were, they would come to see her in the evening, quietly, and talk with her alone by her fire. She could not help knowing that she carried the torch of her beauty with her wherever she went; she carried it high into every room she walked into. And after all, however much she might veil it, and shrink from the monotonous bearing it forced on her, her beauty showed. She had been admired. She had been loved. She had walked into rooms where people sat mourning. Tears had been shed in front of her. Men, and women too, had set aside the multitude of things in their lives and allowed themselves, with her, the relief of simplicity. It wounded her that he should shrink from her. It hurt. And yet it was not a clean hurt, not a right one. That was what bothered her, coming as it did on top of her discontent with her husband: the feeling she had now—as Mr. Carmichael shuffled past, barely nodding in answer to her question, a book under his arm, in his yellow slippers—that she was under suspicion; that all this longing of hers to give, to help, was vanity. Was it for her own gratification that she wanted so instinctively to help, to give, so that people would say of her, “O Mrs. Ramsay! dear Mrs. Ramsay … Mrs. Ramsay, of course!” and need her, and send for her, and admire her? Wasn’t this what she secretly wanted? And so when Mr. Carmichael drew back from her, as he was doing at this very moment, slipping away to some corner where he did his acrostic puzzles endlessly, she felt not simply rebuffed in her instinct, but made aware of the pettiness of some part of herself, and of human relations—how flawed they are, how contemptible, how selfish, even at their best. Worn out and shabby, and presumably no longer (her cheeks were hollow, her hair was white) a sight to fill anyone’s eyes with joy, she had better give her mind to the story of the Fisherman and his Wife, and so calm that bundle of sensitiveness, her son James (none of her children was as sensitive as he was).
danish_before_fix: Han svarede ikke. Han tog opium. Ifølge børnene havde det farvet hans skæg gult. Det havde det måske. Hvad der var tydeligt for hende, var, at den stakkels mand var ulykkelig, og at han kom til dem hvert år for at slippe væk; og alligevel, hvert eneste år, havde hun den samme fornemmelse: at han ikke stolede på hende. Hun ville sige: »Jeg tager ind til byen. Kan jeg hente frimærker, papir, tobak til dig?« og mærke ham krympe sig. Han stolede ikke på hende. Hans kone var skyld i det. Hun huskede den ondskabsfulde måde, hans kone havde behandlet ham på, som havde gjort hende, fru Ramsay, til stål og diamant dér i det forfærdelige lille værelse i St. John's Wood, da hun med egne øjne havde set den afskyelige kvinde vise ham ud af huset. Han var sjusket; han spildte på sin frakke; han havde alle de kedelige vaner, som en gammel mand har, når han ikke har noget at tage sig til i verden; og hans kone viste ham ud af værelset. På sin afskyelige måde sagde hun: »Nu vil fru Ramsay og jeg gerne have en lille snak sammen,« og fru Ramsay kunne se, lige så tydeligt som om det stod lige for hendes øjne, hele hans livs endeløse elendighed. Havde han penge nok til tobak? Måtte han bede sin kone om dem? En halv krone? Atten pence? Åh, hun kunne ikke holde ud at tænke på de små ydmygelser, den kvinde udsatte ham for. Og altid nu (hun kunne ikke gætte hvorfor, medmindre det på en eller anden måde stammede fra den kvinde) veg han tilbage for hende. Han betroede sig aldrig til hende. Og dog, hvad mere kunne hun have gjort? Et solrigt værelse var blevet stillet til hans rådighed. Børnene var venlige over for ham. Aldrig havde hun givet det mindste tegn på, at han var uvelkommen. Tværtimod gjorde hun sig umage for at være venlig. Vil du have frimærker, vil du have tobak? Her er en bog, du måske kunne lide, og så videre. Og når alt kom til alt — når alt kom til alt (her rettede hun sig, uden at være sig det bevidst, op, og følelsen af hendes egen skønhed, så sjældent til stede hos hende, kom over hende nu) — når alt kom til alt, havde hun som regel ikke svært ved at få folk til at kunne lide hende. Der var for eksempel George Manning; hr. Wallace; berømte mænd var de, men de kom og besøgte hende om aftenen, stille, og talte med hende alene ved hendes pejs. Hun kunne ikke lade være med at vide, at hun bar sin skønheds fakkel med sig, hvor hun end gik; hun bar den højt ind i ethvert rum, hun trådte ind i. Og når alt kom til alt, hvor meget hun end tilsløre den og krympede sig ved den ensformige holdning, den tvang hende til, så viste hendes skønhed sig. Hun var blevet beundret. Hun var blevet elsket. Hun var trådt ind i rum, hvor folk sad i sorg. Der var blevet grædt foran hende. Mænd, og kvinder også, havde lagt det mylder af ting, der fyldte deres liv, til side og givet sig selv, sammen med hende, den lettelse, det er at være enkel. Det sårede hende, at han skulle krympe sig for hende. Det gjorde ondt. Og alligevel var det ikke en ren smerte, ikke en retmæssig en. Det var det, der plagede hende, når det nu kom oven i hendes utilfredshed med hendes mand: følelsen, hun havde nu — mens hr. Carmichael slæbte sig forbi, knap nok nikkende som svar på hendes spørgsmål, med en bog under armen, i sine gule tøfler — af at være under mistanke; af at hele hendes længsel efter at give, efter at hjælpe, var forfængelighed. Var det for hendes egen tilfredsstillelses skyld, at hun så instinktivt ville hjælpe, give, så folk kunne sige om hende: »Åh, fru Ramsay! kære fru Ramsay … fru Ramsay, selvfølgelig!« og have brug for hende og sende bud efter hende og beundre hende? Var det ikke det, hun i det skjulte ville have? Og så, da hr. Carmichael trak sig tilbage fra hende, som han gjorde i netop dette øjeblik, og gled af sted til et eller andet hjørne, hvor han endeløst løste sine akrostikoner, følte hun sig ikke blot afvist i sit instinkt, men blev gjort opmærksom på småligheden i en del af sig selv og i menneskelige forhold — hvor mangelfulde de er, hvor foragtelige, hvor selviske, selv når de er bedst. Udslidt og lasket og formodentlig ikke længere (hendes kinder var indsunkne, hendes hår var hvidt) et syn, der kunne fylde nogens øjne med glæde, gjorde hun bedre i at rette sin opmærksomhed mod historien om Fiskeren og hans kone og således berolige det knippe af følsomhed, hendes søn James (ingen af hendes børn var så følsomme som ham).

Og dog, hvad mere kunne hun have gjort? Et solrigt værelse var blevet stillet til hans rådighed. Børnene var venlige over for ham. Aldrig havde hun givet det mindste tegn på, at han var uvelkommen. Tværtimod gjorde hun sig umage for at være venlig. Vil du have frimærker, vil du have tobak? Her er en bog, du måske kunne lide, og så videre. Og når alt kom til alt — når alt kom til alt (her rettede hun sig, uden at være sig det bevidst, op, og følelsen af hendes egen skønhed, så sjældent til stede hos hende, kom over hende nu) — når alt kom til alt, havde hun som regel ikke svært ved at få folk til at kunne lide hende. Der var for eksempel George Manning; hr. Wallace; berømte mænd var de, men de kom og besøgte hende om aftenen, stille, og talte med hende alene ved hendes pejs. Hun kunne ikke lade være med at vide, at hun bar sin skønheds fakkel med sig, hvor hun end gik; hun bar den højt ind i ethvert rum, hun trådte ind i. Og når alt kom til alt, hvor meget hun end tilslørede den og krympede sig ved den ensformige holdning, den tvang hende til, så viste hendes skønhed sig. Hun var blevet beundret. Hun var blevet elsket. Hun var trådt ind i rum, hvor folk sad i sorg. Der var blevet grædt foran hende. Mænd, og kvinder også, havde lagt det mylder af ting, der fyldte deres liv, til side og givet sig selv, sammen med hende, den lettelse, det er at være enkel. Det sårede hende, at han skulle krympe sig for hende. Det gjorde ondt. Og alligevel var det ikke en ren smerte, ikke en rigtig. english: “But the father of eight children has no choice. …” He broke off his half-audible muttering, turned, sighed, lifted his eyes, looked for the figure of his wife reading stories to the little boy, and filled his pipe. He turned his back on the sight of human ignorance and human fate and the sea eating the ground we stand on—a sight which, had he been able to hold his gaze on it, might have led somewhere. And he took comfort in trifles so slight, next to the grand theme he had just been facing, that he was inclined to skip over that comfort, to disown it, as though for an honest man to be caught being happy in a world of misery were the most shameful crime of all. It was true: most of the time he was happy; he had his wife; he had his children; in six weeks he had promised to talk “some nonsense” to the young men of Cardiff about Locke, Hume, Berkeley, and the causes of the French Revolution. But all this, and the pleasure he took in it—in the phrases he turned, in the ardor of the young, in his wife’s beauty, in the tributes that came to him from Swansea, Cardiff, Exeter, Southampton, Kidderminster, Oxford, Cambridge—all of it had to be made light of and hidden under the words “talking nonsense,” because, in effect, he had not done the thing he might have done. It was a disguise. It was where a man took refuge who was afraid to own his own feelings, who could not say, This is what I like—this is what I am. And William Bankes and Lily Briscoe found it rather pitiful and distasteful; they wondered why such concealments were needed; why he always needed praise; why a man so brave in his thinking should be so timid in his living; how oddly he was both venerable and laughable at once.

english: Now it came back to her, what she had meant to say about Mrs. Ramsay. She couldn’t tell how she would have phrased it, but it would have been a criticism. The other night some bit of high-handedness had irritated her. Following the line of Mr. Bankes’s gaze toward Mrs. Ramsay, she thought that no woman could worship another woman as he worshipped her; women could only shelter together in the shade he cast over them both. Following his beam, she added her own, different ray. Mrs. Ramsay, she thought, was without question the loveliest of people (bent over her book there); perhaps the best; but also unlike the perfect form you saw before you. Yet why unlike, and unlike in what way? she wondered, scraping off her palette all those heaps of blue and green, which looked to her now like lifeless lumps of earth—though she swore that tomorrow she would breathe life into them, make them move and flow and obey her. In what way was Mrs. Ramsay different? What was the spirit in her, the essence, so that if you came across a glove tucked into the corner of a sofa you would know from its twisted finger that it was hers, beyond any doubt? For speed she was like a bird; for directness, an arrow. She was headstrong; she was commanding (naturally, Lily reminded herself, I’m thinking of how she is with women, and I’m much younger, a nobody, living off the Brompton Road). She threw open bedroom windows. She shut doors. (In this way Lily tried to get the tune of Mrs. Ramsay started in her head.) She would turn up late at night, tapping lightly on your bedroom door, wrapped in an old fur coat (that was always the setting for her beauty—hurried, but just right), and act out once again whatever it happened to be: Charles Tansley losing his umbrella; Mr. Carmichael snuffling and sniffing; Mr. Bankes announcing, “the vegetable salts are lost.” She would shape it all skillfully, even give it a malicious twist. Then she would move across to the window, pretending she had to go—it was dawn, she could see the sun coming up—and half turn back, more intimate now, yet still always laughing, to insist that she must, Minta must, all of them must marry. Because in the whole world, whatever laurels might be thrown her way (but Mrs. Ramsay didn’t care a fig about Lily’s painting), or whatever triumphs she might win (Mrs. Ramsay had probably had her share of those)—and here she grew sad and dark and returned to her chair—one thing was beyond dispute: an unmarried woman (she took Lily’s hand lightly for a moment), an unmarried woman has missed the best of life. The house seemed full of sleeping children and of Mrs. Ramsay listening; of lamps turned low and steady breathing.

english: What was the child dreaming about? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. She stood there so absorbed in some private thought that the message had to be given twice: go and ask Mildred whether Andrew, Miss Doyle, and Mr. Rayley are back yet. The words seemed to drop into a well whose water, clear as it was, bent things so strangely that you could watch them twisting as they sank, making heaven knows what pattern on the floor of the child’s mind. What message would Cam actually deliver to the cook? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. And in fact it was only by waiting patiently, and hearing all about an old woman in the kitchen with very red cheeks who was drinking soup out of a bowl, that Mrs. Ramsay finally set off that parrot-like instinct in her. It had caught Mildred’s words quite exactly, and could now repeat them, if you were patient, in a flat singsong. Shifting from one foot to the other, Cam recited: “No, they haven’t, and I’ve told Ellen to clear away tea.”

english: Oh, but she never wanted James to get one day older, nor Cam either. These two she would have liked to keep just as they were, forever—demons of wickedness, angels of delight—and never watch them turn into long-legged monsters. Nothing could make up for that loss. Just now, when she had read James the line “and there were numbers of soldiers with kettledrums and trumpets,” and his eyes had darkened, she had thought: why should they grow up and lose all that? Of all her children he was the most gifted, the most sensitive. But every one of them, she thought, was full of promise. Prue was an absolute angel with the others, and these days, especially in the evenings, her beauty could take your breath away. Andrew—even her husband granted that he had an extraordinary gift for mathematics. And Nancy and Roger had both turned into wild creatures, running all over the countryside from morning till night. As for Rose, her mouth was too big, but she was wonderful with her hands. When they put on charades, it was Rose who made the costumes; she made everything; what she liked best was arranging things—tables, flowers, anything at all. Mrs. Ramsay didn’t like Jasper shooting birds; but that was only a phase; they all went through phases. Why, she asked, resting her chin on the top of James’s head, must they grow up so quickly? Why must they go off to school? She would have liked always to have a baby. She was never happier than with one in her arms. Then people could call her tyrannical, domineering, overbearing, whatever they pleased; she didn’t care. And as she touched his hair with her lips she thought, he will never be this happy again—but she stopped herself, remembering how angry her husband got when she said that. Still, it was true. They were happier now than they would ever be again. A tenpenny tea set could keep Cam happy for days. The moment they woke, she heard them stamping and crowing on the floor over her head. They came clattering along the passage. Then the door burst open and in they came, fresh as roses, wide-eyed, wide awake, as if coming into the dining room after breakfast—which they did every single day of their lives—were a real occasion for them. And so it went, one thing after another, all day long, until she went up to say good night and found them caught in their cots like birds netted among the cherries and raspberries, still inventing stories about some scrap of rubbish—something they had overheard, something they had found in the garden. They each had their little treasures. … And so she went downstairs and said to her husband, Why must they grow up and lose it all? They’ll never be so happy again. And he was angry. Why take such a gloomy view of life? he said. It isn’t sensible. For it was strange—and she believed it to be true—that for all his gloom and despair he was happier than she was, more hopeful on the whole. Perhaps it was that he was less exposed to human troubles. He always had his work to fall back on. Not that she was “pessimistic” herself, as he accused her of being. It was only that she thought life—and a small strip of time appeared before her eyes, her fifty years. There it lay in front of her—life. Life, she thought, but she didn’t finish the thought. She took a look at life, because she had a distinct sense of it there, something real, something private, which she shared with neither her children nor her husband. A kind of transaction went on between the two of them, with her on one side and life on the other. She was always trying to get the upper hand of it, as it was of her; and sometimes they held talks (when she sat by herself); there had been, she remembered, great scenes of reconciliation. But mostly, oddly enough, she had to admit that she felt this thing she called life to be terrible, hostile, ready to spring on you the moment you gave it the chance. There were the eternal problems: suffering; death; the poor. Even here there was always some woman dying of cancer. And yet she had told all these children, You shall go through with it. To eight people she had said it, relentlessly (and the greenhouse bill would come to fifty pounds). And for that reason, knowing what lay in store for them—love and ambition and being miserable and alone in dreary places—she often felt: Why must they grow up and lose it all? And then, brandishing her sword at life, she told herself, Nonsense. They’ll be perfectly happy. And here she was, she thought, feeling again that life was rather sinister, making Minta marry Paul Rayley. Because whatever she might feel about her own transaction—and she had been through things that needn’t happen to everyone (she didn’t name them, even to herself)—she was driven on, too fast, she knew, almost as if it were an escape for her as well, to declare that people must marry; people must have children.

Hun var aldrig gladere end med en i sine arme. Så kunne folk kalde hende tyrannisk, herskesyg, myndig, hvad de nu havde lyst til; hun var ligeglad. Og mens hun rørte hans hår med læberne, tænkte hun, han bliver aldrig så lykkelig igen — men hun standsede sig selv, idet hun huskede, hvor vred hendes mand blev, når hun sagde det. Og sådan fortsatte det, det ene efter det andet, hele dagen lang, indtil hun gik op for at sige godnat og fandt dem fanget i deres senge som fugle i net blandt kirsebær og hindbær, mens de stadig fandt på historier om en eller anden stump skrammel — noget, de havde overhørt, noget, de havde fundet i haven. De havde hver deres små skatte. … Og så gik hun nedenunder og sagde til sin mand: Hvorfor skal de vokse op og miste det hele? De bliver aldrig så lykkelige igen. Og han blev vred. Hvorfor have et så dystert syn på livet? sagde han. Det er ikke fornuftigt. For det var mærkeligt — og hun mente, at det var sandt — at han trods al sin dysterhed og fortvivlelse var lykkeligere end hun, mere håbefuld i det store og hele. Måske var det, fordi han var mindre udsat for menneskelige kvaler. Han havde altid sit arbejde at falde tilbage på. Ikke at hun selv var »pessimistisk«, som han beskyldte hende for at være. Det var bare, at hun mente, at livet — og en lille stribe tid viste sig for hendes øjne, hendes halvtreds år. Dér lå det foran hende — livet. Livet, tænkte hun, men hun gjorde ikke tanken færdig. Hun kastede et blik på livet, for hun havde en tydelig fornemmelse af det dér, noget virkeligt, noget privat, som hun hverken delte med sine børn eller sin mand. En slags handel foregik mellem dem to, med hende på den ene side og livet på den anden. Hun forsøgte altid at få overtaget over det, ligesom det over hende; og nogle gange holdt de samtaler (når hun sad alene); der havde været, huskede hun, store forsoningsscener. Men for det meste måtte hun, mærkeligt nok, indrømme, at hun følte, at denne ting, hun kaldte livet, var forfærdelig, fjendtlig, parat til at springe på én i det øjeblik, man gav den chancen. Der var de evige problemer: lidelse; død; de fattige. Selv her var der altid en eller anden kvinde, der lå og døde af kræft. Og alligevel havde hun sagt til alle disse børn: I skal igennem det. Til otte mennesker havde hun sagt det, ubarmhjertigt (og drivhusregningen ville løbe op i halvtreds pund). Og af den grund, fordi hun vidste, hvad der ventede dem — kærlighed og ærgerrighed og at være ulykkelig og alene på triste steder — følte hun ofte: Hvorfor skal de vokse op og miste det hele? Og så, mens hun svingede sit sværd mod livet, sagde hun til sig selv: Sludder. De bliver helt og aldeles lykkelige. Og her var hun, tænkte hun, igen med en følelse af, at livet var temmelig uhyggeligt, i færd med at få Minta til at gifte sig med Paul Rayley. english: She turned the page. Only a few lines were left, so she would finish the story, even though bedtime had passed. It was getting late. She could tell from the light in the garden; and the flowers turning white and something gray in the leaves combined to wake a feeling of anxiety in her. At first she couldn’t think what it was about. Then it came to her: Paul and Minta and Andrew weren’t back. Once more she summoned up the little group on the terrace outside the hall door, standing there looking up at the sky. Andrew had taken his net and basket. That meant he intended to catch crabs and so on. That meant he would clamber out onto some rock and be cut off by the tide. Or, coming home in single file along one of those narrow paths above the cliff, one of them might slip. He would roll, and then crash. It was getting quite dark.

english: No, she thought, gathering up a few of the pictures he had cut out—a refrigerator, a lawn mower, a gentleman in evening dress—children never forget. That was why it mattered so much what you said and what you did, and why it came as a relief when they were in bed. Now she didn’t need to think about anyone. She could be herself, by herself. And lately that was what she often felt the need of—to think; well, not even to think. To be silent; to be alone. All the being and doing, expansive, glittering, talkative, evaporated; and with a sense of solemnity you shrank to being yourself, a wedge-shaped core of darkness, something invisible to others. Though she kept on knitting and sat upright, this was how she felt herself to be; and this self, having shed its attachments, was free for the strangest adventures. When life sank down for a moment, the range of experience seemed to have no limit. And everyone, she supposed, always had this sense of unlimited resources; one after another, she, Lily, Augustus Carmichael, must feel that our apparitions, the things you recognize us by, are simply childish. Underneath, it is all dark, it is all spreading, it is unfathomably deep; but every now and then we rise to the surface, and that is what you see us by. Her horizon seemed to her boundless. There were all the places she had never seen; the plains of India; she felt herself pushing aside the heavy leather curtain at the door of a church in Rome. This core of darkness could go anywhere, because nobody saw it. They couldn’t stop it, she thought, exulting. Here was freedom, here was peace, here was—most welcome of all—a gathering together, a resting on a platform of stability. You never found rest as yourself, in her experience (at this point her needles did something deft), but as a wedge of darkness. Once you lost your personality, you lost the fret, the hurry, the stir. And whenever things came together in this peace, this rest, this eternity, some cry of triumph over life rose to her lips. Pausing there, she looked out to meet that stroke of the Lighthouse, the long steady stroke, the last of the three, which was her stroke. For watching them in this mood, always at this hour, you couldn’t help attaching yourself to one thing above all among the things you saw; and this thing, the long steady stroke, was her stroke. Often she caught herself sitting and looking, sitting and looking, her work in her hands, until she became the thing she was looking at—that light, say. And it would lift up some little phrase or other that had been lying in her mind like that—“Children don’t forget, children don’t forget”—and she would repeat it and start adding to it. It will end, It will end, she said. It will come, it will come, when all at once she added, We are in the hands of the Lord.

Selv om hun blev ved med at strikke og sad rank, var det sådan, hun følte sig selv at være; og dette jeg, der havde kastet sine bindinger af, var frit til de mærkeligste eventyr. Når livet sank sammen et øjeblik, syntes erfaringens rækkevidde at være uden grænser. Og alle, formodede hun, havde altid denne fornemmelse af ubegrænsede ressourcer; den ene efter den anden, hun, Lily, Augustus Carmichael, måtte føle, at vore skikkelser, de ting, man genkender os på, simpelthen er barnagtige. Nedenunder er det hele mørkt, det hele breder sig, det er ufatteligt dybt; men en gang imellem stiger vi op til overfladen, og det er det, man ser os på. Hendes horisont forekom hende grænseløs. Der var alle de steder, hun aldrig havde set; Indiens sletter; hun mærkede, at hun skubbede det tunge læderforhæng til side i døren til en kirke i Rom. Denne kerne af mørke kunne gå overalt hen, fordi ingen så den. De kunne ikke stoppe den, tænkte hun jublende. Her var frihed, her var fred, her var — mest velkomment af alt — en samling, en hvilen på en platform af stabilitet. Man fandt aldrig hvile som sig selv, efter hendes erfaring (på dette sted gjorde hendes pinde noget behændigt), men som en kile af mørke. Når man mistede sin personlighed, mistede man uroen, jagten, røret. Og hver gang tingene faldt sammen i denne fred, denne hvile, denne evighed, steg et sejrsråb over livet op til hendes læber. Hun standsede og så ud for at møde det strøg fra Fyret, det lange, jævne strøg, det sidste af de tre, som var hendes strøg.
